The sand diver Trichonotus filamentosus is a benthic-dwelling teleost that inhabits sandy substrates across the Indo-Pacific region, where it relies on cryptobenthic behaviour to evade predators while ambushing small crustacean prey. Field surveys indicate that reproductively active males attain a standard length at puberty of 7 cm [Lp = 7 cm], a size threshold that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence following a period of somatic growth. At a stable water temperature of 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of mature individuals reaches 5% [GSI = 5%]. This value situates T. filamentosus among congeners that partition reproductive effort across multiple spawning events within a single breeding season rather than concentrating resources into a single, large annual episode. Histological examination of gonadal tissue reveals asynchronous oocyte development, a pattern that supports the interpretation of sustained, repeated gamete release over the reproductive period.

Eggs of Trichonotus filamentosus are small and pelagic, with an average diameter of approximately 0.5 mm, yielding an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.000065 grams [Wwb = 0.000065 grams] per newly released embryo. This minuscule birth mass reflects the energetic economy of producing numerous, small offspring—a strategy that offsets high larval mortality through numerical abundance rather than per-offspring investment. Embryonic development proceeds rapidly under the thermal regime typical of the species' shallow-water habitat, with hatching occurring after only 5 days [ab = 5 days] when incubated at 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C]. Such abbreviated incubation periods are characteristic of small-bodied teleosts that exploit warm, productive nursery environments, where rapid yolk absorption and early transition to exogenous feeding are essential for survival. The resulting yolk-sac larva is endotrophic for a brief interval before commencing first feeding, at which point its dependence on planktonic prey imposes a critical bottleneck on early survival.

Juvenile sand divers grow rapidly following the pelagic larval phase, and available data from captive rearing studies indicate that the species attains an ultimate standard length of 15 cm [Li = 15 cm] in adulthood. This maximum recorded body size appears consistent across much of the known geographic range, suggesting limited phenotypic plasticity in asymptotic length, though local environmental conditions may influence growth trajectory. The corresponding maximum wet weight achieved at this length has been estimated from length–weight regressions as 18.1 grams [Wwi = 18.1 grams], placing Trichonotus filamentosus among the smaller-bodied members of the Trichonotidae. Sexual dimorphism in size is not pronounced, although mature males may develop elongated anterior dorsal-fin rays that serve a display function during courtship, an adaptation that does not appear to confer a substantial somatic cost relative to overall mass. The growth pattern follows a decelerating trajectory typical of determinate-growing teleosts, with most of the asymptotic length achieved within the first year of life.

Sexual maturation in Trichonotus filamentosus involves a protogynous sex-change strategy, wherein individuals initially develop as functional females. The transformation from female to male typically occurs at a standard length of approximately 10 cm, a transition that is not captured by the standard length at puberty value of 7 cm [Lp = 7 cm], which describes the onset of female reproductive capability rather than the later sex change. At the point of puberty, the average wet weight of an individual is 1.7 grams [Wwp = 1.7 grams], a modest body mass that reflects the early allocation of resources to reproductive tissue. This pattern of early female maturation followed by later sex reversal is common among protogynous reef fishes and is thought to arise from the size-advantage model, in which larger individuals gain greater fitness by functioning as males in a polygynous mating system. Field observations confirm that territorial males are invariably the largest fish present on a given sand patch.

The maximum lifespan of Trichonotus filamentosus has been inferred from length-at-age data collected across multiple field sites, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 2555 days [am = approximately 2555 days] under natural conditions at 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to roughly seven years, is relatively extended for a small cryptobenthic fish and may be linked to the species' low natural mortality rate on protected sandy flats. Senescence is not abrupt; rather, older individuals exhibit gradual declines in condition and reproductive output, with the gonado-somatic index decreasing in the oldest age classes. Comparative analysis of conspecific populations at different latitudes suggests that thermal regime exerts a modulating effect on both growth rate and lifespan, with cooler-water individuals potentially living longer but growing more slowly. Future studies examining otolith microstructure could refine age estimation and clarify the environmental correlates of lifespan variation across the species' distribution.
